doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

title: The geography of Chicago music and the West Side blues
summary: Ware describes how the north, west and south sides differed and how blues audiences on the West Side would not take jazz.

story.theme_name: Chicago: the jazz migration and its clubs
story.community_name: Going north: working the Chicago jazz scene

blocks.x: Joe's been on top of the music scene in Chicago for years, you know; like -- see, Chicago was kind of split up. There was the north side, west side, and the south side. You don't really have no east side; it's east now, but all the real, I would say, swinging stuff was out the south side and maybe further north. Got around Argyle then, you know -- Lawrence Avenue, white clubs and what not.

Then on the west side of Chicago, you had all the and Howling Wolf blues joints. That's where Muddy Waters, and all those kind of people -- Blind John, all those people; Willie Dixon, they had that territory. And you would go and play a gig on the west side, and people wouldn't accept you -- there were a few diehard jazz lovers, but if you weren't playing the harmonica, Spitoon Blues, you was in trouble.
